name: The Rieseneiche of the Sauerbusch

location.address: Sauerbusch, Dresdner Heide (forest district Hofewiese), near Langebruck

access: Free. Public forest (Sachsenforst, Dresdner Heide); a signposted educational trail 'Rieseneichen' (run by the Heimatverein Weixdorf) leads to it. Forest paths, no ticket.
transport: Not verified. Remote forest stand in the far north-east of the Heide near Langebruck, well over 30 minutes from the centre; reached on foot or by bike from Langebruck or Weixdorf. Check current timetables before quoting a stop.
verify_notes: Register-only (city Naturdenkmal ND 72; de.wikipedia plus Wikidata coordinate). Tree-level Wikidata coordinate; Commons has CC0 photos of the trunk base and hole taken 2021-05-31 by Pedalito (CC0), so a photo exists; lifecheck RECENT 2025-06-12 near the pin. Conflict on height: de.wikipedia article says about 22 m, the ND list says 14 m; main stem broke off at about 15 m, the crown is single limbs. Girth about 6.60 m at 1.30 m (measured 2016, cited to monumentaltrees on the list page; cross-checked on article). Age 'up to 700 years' is an estimate in the article, not a measured date; keep vague. History: 1679 forest protocol lists two oaks in the Sauerbusch as boundary markers, likely mast trees; both protected 1938 (other sources say 1958); the second oak fell in a fire started by children in 1993. The forest district describes the tree as 'in its last stage of life' although vital; stem has heavy overgrowth, one side nearly debarked, parts stabilised with concrete. Alive as of 2021 photos; recheck. Twin folded: none (the second oak is gone). Lead: a 'Dresdner Heide' walk with the Rotbuche dre_007 (about 5.5 km apart, separate stops).
story:
In 1679 a forest protocol listed two oaks in the Sauerbusch as boundary markers. One of them is still alive. Its main stem broke off at about fifteen metres long ago, so what stands now is a trunk about 6.60 metres round carrying a crown made of single limbs. The local account puts it at up to 700 years, which is an estimate rather than a count; somewhere between four and seven centuries is the honest reading.

The two oaks were probably mast trees, kept for their acorns, and both were placed under protection in 1938, although some sources give 1958. In 1993 a fire started by children killed the second one. This one carried on.

It has not carried on easily. The forest district describes it as being in the last stage of its life, although it is still vital. Heavy growth covers the stem, one side is almost stripped of bark, and parts of it are held together with concrete. Even its height is disputed: the Wikipedia article says about 22 metres, the city's natural monument list says 14.

A signposted trail, the Rieseneichen path kept by the heritage society in Weixdorf, leads through the far north-east of the Dresdner Heide to the trunk. It is a forest walk from Langebruck or Weixdorf rather than a city stroll, and this oak is the reason to make it.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the snapped-off main stem on a trunk about 6.60 metres round, one side almost bare of bark and patched with concrete. It stands on the signposted Rieseneichen trail in the Sauerbusch.

name: The Rotbuche of the Dresdner Heide

location.address: Dresdner Heide, forest section 109 (Revier Langebruck), about 150 m north-west of the crossing of Radeberger Strasse and Schneise 8

access: Free. Stands in the public forest of the Dresdner Heide (Sachsenforst), a short way off the Schneise 8 forest ride; no entry charge.
transport: Not verified. Inside the Heide, over 30 minutes from the centre; reached on foot from the Radeberger Strasse side. Check timetables before quoting a stop.
verify_notes: Register only (city Naturdenkmal ND 108, designated Dec 2000). Wikidata coordinate 51.09819,13.849767 agrees with the de.wikipedia description (150 m NW of the Radeberger Strasse / Schneise 8 crossing) only in prose, which I did not measure, so precision is stated approximate. Photos on Commons: CC BY-SA 3.0 by Dr. Bernd Gross (2015-05-26, 22 files) and CC BY-SA 4.0 Staubi59 (2017). lifecheck on the pin returned NONE. Measurements at designation in 2000: height about 35 m, girth 5.70 m, crown diameter about 28 m. After an unseen fork defect plus a hurricane in October 2002 more than a third of the crown broke off, so today's tree is lower and lopsided; the 35 m figure is the pre-2002 height. The photos show the tree after the damage, which a writer should check. Age 250 years was an estimate in 2000. At designation only the beech behind the Weisses Schloss in Cossebaude (ND 66) was a bigger beech in Dresden. Protected zone 18 m around the trunk.
story:
In October 2002 a hurricane found a fork in this beech that nobody knew was failing, and more than a third of the crown came down. Two years earlier Dresden had made it a natural monument, measured at about 35 metres tall, 5.70 metres round and with a crown some 28 metres across. At that point only one beech in the city was bigger, the one behind the Weisses Schloss in Cossebaude.

What stands in forest section 109 of the Dresdner Heide today is the tree that came out of that storm: lower than the 35 metres in the record and lopsided where the crown went. Every photograph on file was taken after the damage, so they show the beech as a visitor will meet it rather than as it looked on the day it was designated.

The age given in 2000 was about 250 years, and that was an estimate then. Add the years since and it lands somewhere around 275, give or take a few decades. The ordinance protects a ring of 18 metres around the trunk along with the tree itself.

It stands a short way into the forest, about 150 metres north-west of the point where Radeberger Strasse crosses the forest ride called Schneise 8. Our pin is approximate, so expect to look around for the broken crown once you reach the crossing.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the lopsided crown, more than a third of it lost to a storm in 2002, above a trunk about 5.70 metres round. It stands about 150 metres north-west of where Radeberger Strasse crosses Schneise 8.

name: The Oak of Barnsdorfer Strasse

location.address: Junction of Weinbohlaer Strasse and Barnsdorfer Strasse, Leipziger Vorstadt

access: Free. A freestanding tree at a street junction on public ground.
transport: Not verified in detail; inner-city district north-west of the Neustadt, on the B170 side near Hansastrasse. Check the nearest tram stop before quoting.
verify_notes: Register only (city Naturdenkmal ND 29, protected 3 Jan 1985, resolution 266/85). Tree-level Wikidata coordinate; de.wikipedia places it at the southern fork of Weinbohlaer and Barnsdorfer Strasse, about 100 m south-east of the Hechtstrasse turn-off from Hansastrasse, which fits the pin. Photos: 8 files CC BY-SA 3.0 Dr. Bernd Gross, 2015-05-20. lifecheck on the pin returned NONE and the newest photo is 2015, so alive confirmation is thin: flagged. Height about 25 m, crown about 30 m, girth 4.45 m (register). Planted about 1880, probably in the beer garden of the pub 'Zur Gruenen Aue' on the road tip, which stood until 1960 (article says 'vermutlich', so keep hedged; do not bridge it into fact). About 150 m north-east, in the St.-Pauli-Friedhof, stand the Marschall oak and Meschwitz oak, planted c.1870/80 and treated as Dresden memorial trees (Wikidata Q109422836, Q124842660): possible cluster, not verified as accessible here. Protected the same day as the Doebelner Strasse oak, the Kaditzer Linde (dre_005) and the Heide pine.
story:
This oak probably started out in a beer garden. It was planted around 1880 on the tip of land where Weinbohlaer Strasse and Barnsdorfer Strasse fork, and the pub on that tip, Zur Gruenen Aue, stood until 1960. The written record says the tree was probably part of the pub's garden, and nobody has managed to get further than probably. The pub is gone. The oak, about 140 years old, has outlasted it by more than sixty years.

It has grown to about 25 metres with a crown some 30 metres wide, and its trunk measures 4.45 metres round. Dresden made it a natural monument on 3 January 1985, the same day the city protected the Kaditzer Linde, an oak on Doebelner Strasse and a pine in the Heide.

About 150 metres to the north-east, in the St.-Pauli-Friedhof, stand two more oaks of the same generation, the Marschall oak and the Meschwitz oak, planted around 1870 or 1880 and treated by the city as memorial trees. We have not checked how freely the cemetery can be walked, so this page sends you only to the junction.

The newest photographs of this oak date from 2015, and we have no recent confirmation that it is still in good health. If you pass the fork and it is standing, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the freestanding oak, 4.45 metres round, on the tip of land where Weinbohlaer Strasse and Barnsdorfer Strasse fork. It stands about 100 metres south-east of where Hechtstrasse leaves Hansastrasse.

name: The Linden on the Laubegast Riverbank

location.address: Laubegaster Ufer, by house no. 17, Altlaubegast

access: Free. Stands on the outside of the ice-protection wall of Laubegaster Ufer 17, beside the road; just north of the driveway the road is closed to cars and is a foot and cycle path forming part of the left-bank Elbe cycle route.
transport: Not verified; Laubegast is an eastern Elbe-bank district. Check the nearest tram stop and walking time before quoting.
verify_notes: Register (city Naturdenkmal ND 89, protected 10 June 1999) plus the owner's 1997 letter quoted on de.wikipedia. Coordinates: de.wikipedia list 51/1/30.95N 13/50/23.9E (=51.02582, 13.83997), Wikidata Q124719169 51.0253,13.839993; they agree within about 70 m, so I used the list value which is described as 'by Nr. 17'; stated confirmed because the tree is on the Elbe path next to a named house, but a writer could re-read the Wikidata offset. Alive: Commons photo 2025-12-27 by Z thomas (CC BY 4.0) and 2024-05-09 lifecheck RECENT. Girth 3.90 m, height about 20 m, crown about 16 m. Age: article says planted or sown in the second half of the 17th century, narrowing to the 1670s or 1680, and the owner wrote of a '320 year old' linden in 1997. The owner built a protective masonry surround in 1913. In March 1940 the largest Elbe flood of the 20th century drove 40 cm ice floes against the wall and tree for 10 to 15 hours, leaving a wound about 50 cm tall around half the trunk; a ridge at roughly 1.5 m height still shows it. Pavement around the roots was replaced with cobbles to protect it. The house behind was built 1879 for a Saxon court marshal (protected Kulturdenkmal). Two other Laubegast ND trees stand about 500 m each way (black poplars at no. 1, black pine at no. 39), same cycle path. Photos CC BY-SA 3.0 Dr. Bernd Gross 2014/2015.
story:
In March 1940 the biggest Elbe flood of the twentieth century drove ice floes 40 centimetres thick against this lime for ten to fifteen hours. The floes hit both the tree and the masonry surround its owner had built in 1913. The ice tore a wound about half a metre tall around half the trunk, and the ridge it left still shows at roughly 1.5 metres up.

The lime was already old by then. The local account has it planted or sown in the second half of the seventeenth century, most likely in the 1670s or around 1680, and in 1997 the owner wrote of a 320-year-old linden. That puts it somewhere near 340 today. The house behind it at number 17 is a youngster by comparison, built in 1879 for a Saxon court marshal and now a listed monument in its own right.

It is a small-leaved lime, about 20 metres tall with a trunk 3.90 metres round, standing outside the ice-protection wall beside the road. The paving over its roots was replaced with cobbles to protect them, and the city made it a natural monument in June 1999.

Just north of the driveway the road closes to cars and becomes part of the Elbe cycle route, and two more protected trees stand about 500 metres away in each direction along it: black poplars at number 1 and a black pine at number 39.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the old ice wound, a ridge at about 1.5 metres on a trunk 3.90 metres round. It stands by the road outside the wall of Laubegaster Ufer 17.

best_time.label: July, when it flowers and the riverbank smells of lime blossom

name: The Fluttering Elm of Konigsbrucker Strasse

location.address: Konigsbrucker Strasse 49, on the pavement side between houses 49 and 51, Aussere Neustadt

access: Free. The elm stands on the pavement side of the property in front of the houses at Konigsbrucker Strasse 49 to 51 and is visible and reachable from the public pavement on a main street; the pin marks the tree on the street frontage.
transport: Not verified in detail; Aussere Neustadt on the Konigsbrucker Strasse tram corridor, close to the centre. Check the nearest stop before quoting.
verify_notes: Register (city Naturdenkmal ND 131, ordinance January 2015). Wikidata coordinate 51.07062119,13.74958807 matches the ND list value 51/4/14.05N 13/44/59.05E (=51.07057, 13.74974), two independent entries within about 15 m. Photos: 5 files CC BY-SA 3.0 Z thomas 2018-05-28 and 7 files 2019-05-06/07, plus Dr. Bernd Gross 2015. lifecheck says OLD (2011 file) but the Commons upload dates show 2018/2019; newest photo 2019, so alive-now is thin: flagged. Measurements per de.wikipedia: height about 30 m, crown about 20 m, girth 3.57 m. Why it was chosen: in the early 2010s the city put forward 39 especially valuable trees at 29 sites for protection; this elm was picked because European elm species are threatened by Dutch elm disease from Asian fungi and this exceptional specimen is healthy and defines the streetscape. Flatter-Ulme Altubigau and the Sachsenplatz elms had been protected since 1999. No age is documented; leave empty and let the page ask. Possible access caveat: the tree is on the property frontage 'gehwegseitig vorgelagert' (pavement-side), which I read as public pavement; I could not check the plot boundary on the ground.
story:
Dresden protected this elm in 2015 for surviving something most of its kind have not. Dutch elm disease, spread by fungi that arrived from Asia, has killed elms across Europe, and when the city went looking in the early 2010s for its most valuable trees, 39 of them at 29 sites, it picked this European white elm as an exceptional specimen that was still healthy.

It is not a park tree. It stands on Konigsbrucker Strasse in the Aussere Neustadt, on the pavement side in front of numbers 49 and 51, and it sets the look of the street: about 30 metres tall, with a crown some 20 metres across and a trunk 3.57 metres round. Trams run past it along the Konigsbrucker Strasse corridor.

It was not the city's first protected elm. A white elm in Altubigau and the elms on Sachsenplatz had been natural monuments since 1999, so this one joined a short list rather than starting it.

Two things we do not know. Nobody has documented when it was planted, so this page gives no age; if you know, tell us. And the newest photographs on record are from 2019, so if you walk past and it is still standing over the pavement, that is worth a message too.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the tall elm, about 30 metres, on the pavement side of Konigsbrucker Strasse in front of numbers 49 and 51. Its trunk measures 3.57 metres round.

name: The Sängereiche on the Elbe Meadows

location.address: Elbwiesen (Waldschlösschenwiese), beside the Waldschlösschenbrücke and the Körnerweg / Elbe cycle path, Radeberger Vorstadt

Several unnamed OSM trees stand 20 to 50 m away, which is why the named node and photo description carry the pin. Facts (de.wikipedia, citing Ostdeutsches Baumarchiv): memorial oak for the first German Sängerbundesfest, July 1865 (Dresden); planted 13 Nov 1865 where the festival hall had stood, by Heinrich Hartwig with two gardeners. 1994: height 26 m, crown 20 m, girth 3.80 m; 2018 girth 4.26 m (girth_cm 426 is the 2018 figure; height_m 26 is the 1994 figure). The 1925 festival booklet says the November 1865 tree was the original gift (Leipzig-area choirs carried a young oak in a tub in the procession) and that a replanting was later needed after vandalism; Rainer Pfannkuchen (ex head of Dresden's nature-protection authority, Elbhang-Kurier April 2021) thinks the original died of drought and the 1865 planting was already a replacement. So the age basis is the documented November 1865 planting, but whether today's trunk is that planting or a later replacement is disputed in the sources: say so, keep the age as an estimate. Alive: photographed 2022 (Commons geotag), girth measured 2018, discussed 2021. lifecheck.py returned OLD (2010) only because it sees bridge-construction photos; the 2022 Commons file is the better evidence. The Waldschlösschenbrücke opened 2013 and the tree stands about 25 m from it. No official register: dewiki plus OSM plus Commons, flagged.
story:
This oak was planted for a song festival, and the sources still argue over whether it is the oak they planted. In July 1865 Dresden hosted the first German Sängerbundesfest, and a festival hall went up on this stretch of the Elbe meadows. On 13 November that year, according to the Ostdeutsches Baumarchiv, Heinrich Hartwig and two gardeners planted a memorial oak where the hall had stood.

That is where the agreement ends. A festival booklet from 1925 says the November tree was the singers' own gift, a young oak that choirs from around Leipzig had carried through the procession in a tub, and that it later had to be replaced after vandals got to it. Rainer Pfannkuchen, once head of Dresden's nature-protection authority, reads it the other way: the festival oak died of drought, and the November 1865 planting was already the replacement. So the trunk in front of you is either the 1865 tree, which would make it about 160 years old, or a later stand-in, and nobody has settled which.

Whichever it is, the open ground has suited it. In 1994 it stood 26 metres tall under a crown 20 metres wide, and its girth grew from 3.80 to 4.26 metres between 1994 and 2018. Since 2013 it has had a neighbour it never asked for: the Waldschlösschenbrücke now crosses the river about 25 metres away, and the Elbe cycle path runs past its feet.

name: The Luther Oak of the Dresdner Heide

location.address: Prinzeß-Margarethen-Park, Dresdner Heide, south of Radeberger Landstrasse between forest rides 17 and 18 (Doppel-E to the north, Alte Acht to the south), Forstabteilung 68, Revier Bühlau

access: Free. Stands in the public forest of the Dresdner Heide (Sachsenforst) beside a forest ride, with a memorial stone, two benches and a table; open at all times.
transport: Not verified. About 850 m east of the Fischhaus in the Albertpark and south of Radeberger Landstrasse; likely over 30 minutes from the centre by bus and foot, check timetables before quoting a stop.

photo_candidate.note: Shows the oak with memorial stone and benches (Feb 2017, leafless). Also File:Luthereiche - panoramio.jpg (CC BY-SA 3.0, geotag 51.074667,13.806833, 24 March 2011, 12 m from the pin; check the exact photographer credit on the file page). Not viewed by me; the viewing pass must look at the pixels.

how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the memorial stone with a Luther inscription at its foot, with two benches and a table beside it. It stands on a forest ride in the Prinzeß-Margarethen-Park part of the Heide.

A geotagged 2011 Commons photo captioned as this tree lies 12 m from the node, and the memorial stone stands beside the tree. Facts (dewiki, citing local sources): planted Sunday 28 Oct 1917 for the 400th anniversary of the Reformation (Luther's 95 Theses); Saxon Kulturdenkmal (ID 09217019) together with the memorial stone. Soil is dry sand over Lusatian granite, so the oak did poorly: called a 'mickriges Exemplar' (puny specimen) in 2017 coverage, so it is NOT a big tree; its worth is the memorial and the setting. Benches renewed and a table added in the 2017 Luther year; one bench carries a Luther quote. Species known only as oak; species not established. Age is the documented 1917 planting of this tree (about 109 years in 2026). No girth or height found. Alive: photographed Feb 2017 and described as living in 2017 coverage; lifecheck not run. One source cluster (dewiki plus OSM plus Commons): flagged. Marginal on worth the walk: young and slight trunk, a lead-grade tree if the photo viewing pass finds it dull.
story:
This oak was planted to honour four hundred years of the Reformation, and it has spent a century failing to look the part. On Sunday 28 October 1917, with Germany deep in the First World War, it went into the ground in the Dresdner Heide to mark the anniversary of Luther's 95 Theses. A memorial stone carrying a Luther inscription was set beside it, and the two together are now a protected Saxon cultural monument, number 09217019.

The ground was against it from the start. This corner of the forest is dry sand over Lusatian granite, and the oak never thrived: local coverage in 2017 called it a puny specimen, which is fair. Nobody comes here for the size of the trunk. What makes it worth the detour is the setting, beside a forest ride in the Prinzeß-Margarethen-Park section of the forest, and the small act of remembrance that keeps being renewed around it. For the Luther year of 2017 the benches were replaced and a table added, and one of the benches now carries a quotation from Luther himself.

It makes a good stop on a walk through the Heide rather than a destination of its own. Two things nobody has recorded: which species of oak it is, and how big it has managed to grow. If you know either, tell us.

story:
The stone beside this oak has changed its mind about who it honours. The tree was planted in 1895 for Otto von Bismarck's 80th birthday, and the sandstone block next to it was dedicated to him too, with his portrait in a bronze medallion. The medallion went missing shortly after the Second World War. In 1998 the block was given a new bronze plaque, this time remembering Hofgärtner H. S. Neumann, 1829 to 1880, the court gardener who designed the Waldpark itself.

So the oak has outlasted the man it was planted for and the monument that explained it. At about 130 years old it is no giant, and nobody has published its girth or height. What it offers is the park its stone now commemorates, and a small lesson in how a memorial gets rewritten when the century moves on.

Be warned before you go: there is no information sign, and the Bismarck Oak stands as part of a group of trees. Our pin is approximate, close to the spot but not on the trunk, so you will have to pick the right oak yourself. The stone is the giveaway. Find the sandstone block with the Neumann plaque on the Lothringer Weg, west of the tennis courts, and the oak is the one beside it.

name: The Pillnitz Camellia

location.address: Kamelienhaus, Schloss und Park Pillnitz, August-Böckstiegel-Straße 2, 01326 Dresden

access: Inside Schloss & Park Pillnitz (owner Staatliche Schloesser, Burgen und Gaerten Sachsen). The camellia stands in its own glass house, open to visitors only in the bloom season, 28 Feb to 12 Apr 2026, daily 10:00-17:00; EUR 5 until 27 March (camellia and palm house), then included in the EUR 8 Schloss & Park Pillnitz ticket. From May to the autumn the glass house is rolled aside and the tree stands in the park; October to May it is inside the heated house.
transport: Schloss Pillnitz, about 12 km upriver (east) of the Altstadt; the Elbe paddle steamers call at Pillnitz. We have not timed the bus route, so check the DVB journey planner before you go.
verify_notes: Alive: the owner's press release of 16 May 2025 (ICS title 'Historische Kamelie', first German camellia so honoured) and the 2026 bloom-season programme; lifecheck RECENT (iNaturalist obs 2026-05-28 at the spot). Pin: five Commons files geotagged 3-22 m from 51.0117,13.8695 depict the Kamelienhaus (a 13 m high rolling glass house, unmistakable); the tree is inside it. Size per owner: 'ueber 250 Jahre alt', 'fast neun Meter hoch'; de.wikipedia adds crown diameter almost 11 m, up to 35,000 crimson single flowers Feb-April. Documented fact: planted at this spot in 1801 by gardener Carl Adolph Terscheck; reached the Dresden court between 1770 and 1790 (so 225+ years at this spot is documented, 250 is the owner's figure). The popular legend that it is one of four plants Thunberg brought from Japan 1775-76 is increasingly doubted (no Kew record); do NOT state it as fact. Genetic study (TU Dresden 2015) found near-identity with the old camellias of Caserta, Campobello (PT) and Greifswald, pointing to vegetative propagation from one stock. Anecdote: wooden winter house burned down in early January 1905 at about -20 C, the firefighting water froze into an ice shell and the plant survived and re-sprouted in spring. Current glass house inaugurated 1992, 13.2 m high, 54 t, 1864 m3, heated to 4-6 C, runs on rails (track gauge 10,800 mm). Claims 'largest and oldest of its kind north of the Alps' is the owner's wording. No girth recorded: multi-stem shrub-tree, only height and crown given. Species is a large evergreen shrub grown as a tree; flag for the writer to say 'camellia tree'. Best time: March main bloom (owner: first buds mid/late Feb, main bloom March, last blooms early/mid April). Photo exists: Commons 'Dresden-Pillnitz, Schloss, die Kamelie.jpg' (CC BY 3.0, user Dguendel, geotagged 14 m away) and others; photo not judged by this pass. Register: not a Naturdenkmal; owner-published tree (counts per BRIEF_RESEARCH). Distance: Pillnitz is outside the walkable centre, label honestly as a Pillnitz stop.

best_time.label: March, when the glass house opens and up to 35,000 crimson flowers are out

how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the 13-metre glass house on rails that covers it from October to May. In summer the house is rolled aside and it stands in the open park beside its tracks, a dark evergreen dome almost nine metres high.
story:
In January 1905 this camellia's winter house burned down at about minus 20 degrees, and the water from the fire hoses froze around the plant in a shell of ice. It survived, and sprouted again that spring.

It has stood on this spot since 1801, when the court gardener Carl Adolph Terscheck planted it. The camellia reached the Dresden court somewhere between 1770 and 1790, so 225 years at Pillnitz are documented; the palace's owners, the Saxon state palaces administration, put it at over 250. A favourite story says it is one of four plants the botanist Carl Peter Thunberg brought back from Japan in the 1770s. Kew has no record of that, and the claim is increasingly doubted. A 2015 study at TU Dresden found it almost genetically identical to the old camellias of Caserta, Campobello in Portugal and Greifswald, which points to cuttings from one shared stock.

Strictly it is a shrub grown into a tree: almost nine metres high, with a crown nearly eleven metres across. In 2025 it became the first camellia in Germany to be named a Historic Camellia by the International Camellia Society.

From October to May it lives inside a heated 13-metre glass house that weighs 54 tonnes and runs on rails. In summer the house rolls aside and the tree stands in the open park. The owners call it the largest and oldest of its kind north of the Alps. Come in March, when up to 35,000 crimson flowers are open.

story:
Legend says that when this poplar blooms, a war is about to end. People reported it in 1870, in 1918 and in 1943, when Victor Klemperer noted it in his diary on 23 May. What appears is not really a bloom but the fluffy white seed of the ripe fruit, and it does not come every year.

The landowner Johann Gottlieb Becke planted the black poplar in 1808 to mark the edge of his property. By 1884 it drew so many visitors that a farmer wanted it felled to keep them off his land, and the local mountain club bought the tree for 300 marks to save it. A viewing frame went up beside it the following year and has been rebuilt in 1922, 1963 and 1999. In the war of 1866 it served as a lookout, and surveyors used it as a sighting mark.

The weather has been harder on it than people were. A thunderstorm on 20 July 1967 took a third of the crown, storms in 1996 took most of the rest, and the main stems were later topped. The 2025 survey gives 15 metres of height where 2004 recorded 26, a trunk 5.50 metres round, and only a few side branches still in leaf. A clone grown from its cuttings was planted a few metres away in 2006, in case.

It stands alone on an open plateau outside the city, and the platform looks over the Elbe valley to Saxon Switzerland and the Ore Mountains.

story:
In the early 1970s a new clinic in Blasewitz was moved 25 metres to spare this tree. The polyclinic had been drawn on the axis of Villa Marienlust, which meant the copper beech in its garden would have had to come down. Volunteer conservationists negotiated, the building went up further south-east with an angled wing to join it to the villa, and the change cost 30,000 marks, judged at the time a great but necessary sacrifice.

The beech was planted in 1849, already four years old, in the villa's 17,000 square metre grounds. The villa now houses a medical centre, the Ärztehaus Blasewitz, whose own history page counts more than 177 years. It has grown about 25 metres tall, with a crown about 24 metres across, so broad and low that it is said to grow like a giant shrub. The register gives its girth as 5.35 metres, but that was measured 30 centimetres above the ground, where any trunk is wider than at the usual chest height.

The city made it natural monument number 34 in January 1985, and a plaque on the tree says so. It stands in the medical centre's garden. The crown can be seen from Naumannstrasse, and we have not confirmed whether the garden is open to walk into; if you have been in, tell us. The surviving oak of Hüblerstrasse stands about 450 metres to the south-west.

name: The Last Oak of Hueblerstrasse

location.address: Hueblerstrasse 23 (street verge), 01309 Dresden

access: Free, on the public street verge of Hueblerstrasse, between two listed villas; no entry needed.
transport: About 300 m west of Schillerplatz in Blasewitz, near the Blue Wonder bridge. We have not checked the nearest tram stop.
verify_notes: THIS IS ONE TREE NOW, not the pair. Natural monument ND 35 listed 'Stieleichen Hueblerstrasse' (Baumgruppe, 2 oaks), pair protected since 22 Aug 1938 and by council ruling 3 Jan 1985. One of the two was felled on 22 June 2025 because of fungi, viruses and bacteria and lost stability (dawo-dresden.de, de.wikipedia; the city's press release pm_067 exists, but the page returned HTTP 503 so was not read; the headline '375 Jahre alte Eiche verliert Kampf gegen Pilz' came through search only). dawo-dresden.de: 'Nur wenige Meter von der gefaellten Eiche steht noch ihr gesunder Baumbruder, der ebenfalls um 1650 gepflanzt wurde' (healthy). The city plans a replacement of a more climate-adapted oak species in autumn 2025 or spring 2026 (so a young tree may now stand beside it; the writer should not confuse them). The writer must make clear that the page is about the surviving one, and that the felled one was its twin. Figures (de.wikipedia, before the felling, for the pair): height about 23 m, crown diameter about 22 m, girths 4.65 m and 4.80 m: I could not establish which girth belongs to the survivor, so girth_cm 480 is the larger of the two and is approximate; do not state a girth for the survivor with precision. Age: a resistograph measurement in 1995 suggests the trees stood by 1650 (wikipedia); the press and dawo say 'planted around 1650' and '375 years'. That is a derived, not a documented, figure, so 350-400 is the honest band. Alive: lifecheck RECENT, Commons photos of Hueblerstrasse 23/25 dated 2025-09-03 (after the felling) and a Commons photo of the felled stump 2025-07-13. Pin: the register coordinate 51.050885,13.802852 and 10+ Commons files geotagged within 12 m; two oaks stood a few metres apart on the verge, one remains, so the pin is on the spot to within metres; the visitor will see the remaining oak and the stump or new planting. Story material: until 1998 the oaks stood with half their trunks in the roadway; protection discs were built in 1998 and the soil to 60 cm depth replaced with a suction vehicle, which uncovered an old granite-paved road half a metre down beside the oaks; root bridges at neighbouring driveways, crown care. The oaks predate the villa district: around 1866 the surroundings were still unbuilt and the road was the old route Striesen-Blasewitz-Loschwitz; the crown form suggests they once stood free and served for acorn mast. The house at Hueblerstrasse 23 was destroyed in WW2 while the oaks survived, between listed villas 21a and 25. Photos: Commons category Naturdenkmal Stieleichen Hueblerstrasse Dresden (files from before 2025 show both oaks; a post-felling file 2025-09-03 shows the survivor); not judged by this pass. Cluster partner: the copper beech of Naumannstrasse 3 (dre_016) is about 450 m north-east.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the one standing oak on the Hüblerstrasse verge, between the villas at numbers 21a and 25. A few metres away is the stump of its felled twin, or the young oak planted to replace it.
story:
Until June 2025 there were two of them. These pedunculate oaks stood a few metres apart on the verge of Hüblerstrasse for something like 375 years, until fungi, viruses and bacteria left one unstable and it was felled on 22 June. This is the survivor, which the local press called its healthy brother. The stump of the twin stands beside it, and the city planned to plant a young oak of a more climate-tolerant kind in its place.

The age comes from a resistograph test in 1995 that suggested the pair already stood by 1650, so read it as somewhere between 350 and 400 years rather than a birth certificate. Either way they are older than the villa quarter around them. Around 1866 this was still open ground and the road was the old route from Striesen through Blasewitz to Loschwitz; the shape of the crowns suggests the oaks once stood free, perhaps kept for their acorns to fatten pigs. The house at number 23 was destroyed in the Second World War. The oaks came through.

Until 1998 they stood with half their trunks in the roadway. That year protective barriers went in, root bridges were laid at the neighbouring driveways, and the soil was replaced to 60 centimetres with a suction vehicle, which uncovered an old granite road half a metre down. Before the felling they were about 23 metres tall, with trunks of 4.65 and 4.80 metres; nobody recorded which girth belongs to the survivor.

Legends (all three reported by de.wikipedia, none documented): a girl abducted by a dragon whose five brothers died looking for her and who planted the trees in their memory; six monks from Kloster Altzella planted six chestnuts before a crusade, only five grew and only five monks came home; five brothers who went out into the world and returned rich, each planting a tree. Stadtwiki: they replaced five lindens that were sacred to the Nisan people at the Gertrud spring (a spring shrine); this is a Stadtwiki claim only, treat as folklore. The lane and the stream (Fuenf-Brueder-Bach) are named after the group. how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the five old chestnut trunks lining the Fünf-Brüder-Weg where it leaves the village for the Tännichtgrund, beside the natural monument sign. The thickest is 6.20 metres round.
story:
Nobody agrees why there are five. One legend has a girl carried off by a dragon and her five brothers dying in the search for her, with the trees planted in their memory. Another has six monks from Altzella monastery planting six chestnuts before a crusade: five grew, and five monks came home. A third has five brothers who went out into the world, came back rich and planted a tree each. Dresden's city wiki adds that they replaced five limes at a spring once sacred to the Slavic Nisani, which is folklore too.

What the sources do agree on is the date, the first half of the 17th century, which makes these sweet chestnuts roughly 400 years old. They stand along a lane at the edge of Oberwartha, on the far western rim of Dresden, where it runs down into the Tännichtgrund valley. The lane is the Fünf-Brüder-Weg and the stream below is the Fünf-Brüder-Bach, both named after the trees, which tells you how long they have been the landmark here.

They run from 12 to 25 metres tall, with crowns 10 to 20 metres across, and their trunks measure between 4.15 and 6.20 metres round at chest height. The group is a protected natural monument, signposted beside the lane. Come in October, when the chestnuts drop.

story:
This oak was planted as a birthday present for a king, and has spent most of its life negotiating with traffic. It went into the ground on Wasaplatz in Strehlen in April 1898, on the 23rd or the 24th depending on which record you trust, for King Albert of Saxony's 70th birthday and his 25th year on the throne. Several Albert oaks went in around Dresden for that double jubilee. This one got a fenced decorative plot ringed with birches.

The square did not stay quiet. A tram line has run through Wasaplatz since 1928, a main road now presses hard against one side of the tree, and its crown is pruned back regularly so that traffic clears it. In 1991 a cable was laid through its root zone and the roots were cut. It kept growing anyway. The most recent measurements put it at about 21 metres tall, with a crown some 24 metres across and a trunk 3.85 metres round; the city's older designation figures give 20 metres and 3.65.

Dresden made it a natural monument in 1999. At under 130 years it is not an ancient tree and does not pretend to be. It is a royal anniversary that kept its leaves, holding the middle of a busy junction while the city works around it.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the single large oak in the middle of the star-shaped Wasaplatz, its trunk 3.85 metres round, with tram tracks curving past. A main road runs hard against one side of it.

story:
This oak is wider than it is tall: when it was measured in 1999 its crown spread about 28 metres across, on a tree about 25 metres high. It stands on what was once the village green of Bühlau, beside Quohrener Strasse, and a few metres to its south-east a small stream, the Quohrener Abzugsgraben, rises out of the ground.

It is not a veteran. The city's 2008 brochure on its natural monuments put it at about 140 years, which places its planting somewhere around the 1860s or 1870s. That is an estimate, not a record, and nobody has written down who planted it or why.

Dresden protected it in 1999, and the ordinance gives three reasons: its particular form and character, what it does for the look of the place, and dendrological grounds. At designation the trunk was 1.26 metres thick at a metre off the ground, about 3.95 metres round; the city's own list gives 4.00.

Two things we would like help with. The pin is approximate: two published coordinates for this tree sit about 60 metres apart, and ours is the one beside the spring. And the most recent dated photographs of it we know of were taken in May 2015. If you have stood under it since, tell us it is still there, and where exactly.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its crown, about 28 metres across and wider than the tree is tall. It stands on the old village green beside Quohrener Strasse, a few metres north-west of where the Quohren stream rises.

story:
This horse chestnut belongs to a variety that normally grows as a shrub, and it is about 20 metres tall. 'Digitata', the fingered-leaf form, has been spreading out of France since 1864. This specimen was grafted onto an ordinary horse chestnut, and above the graft it has gone on to raise a trunk of its own, under a crown about 18 metres wide.

It came out of the Reichsgartenschau of 1936, the national garden show Dresden hosted that year, as one of the rare trees the exhibitors left to the city when the show was over. No planting year was written down, so its age of about 90 is counted from the show rather than from a record of the day it went in.

In January 1985 Dresden's council made it a natural monument, and it was the only tree from the then district of Dresden-Süd in that resolution. The city's documentation gives its trunk as 3.05 metres round at 0.7 metres up; the German Dendrological Society's list of record trees has it at 3.53 metres at breast height in 2010.

It stands in the north-west corner of Volkspark Räcknitz, at the edge of the raised lawn just inside the entrance from Stadtgutstrasse. A garden show lasts a summer. Its shrub that turned into a tree is still here, ninety years on.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its fingered leaves, the rare 'Digitata' form, and the multi-stemmed crown above a grafted trunk. It stands at the edge of the raised lawn just north of the Stadtgutstrasse entrance.

story:
This oak is protected less for its size than for the way it looks beside a pond. It stands on open land west of Langebrück, beside the Brauteich, a pond fed by a stream called the Braugraben, and it is the picture the two make together that the city's documentation singles out: the tree's form, and its interplay with the water.

It has been on the books since 1958, when the district council of Dresden registered two natural monuments at Langebrück, this oak and a spring pond, the Quellteich. The figures are respectable rather than record-breaking. The city gives a height of about 22 metres, a crown about 20 metres across and a trunk 4.70 metres round, less massive than the Albert oak at Kauscha. And the form that earned it protection has had a hard time since: rot and a lightning strike have broken out part of the crown.

Nobody has recorded its age, and the history of the tree is described as largely unknown. If you know when it was planted, or own an old photograph that shows it, tell us.

In 2008 the city put it on a walking and cycling route past five natural monuments in Dresden's north, together with the giant oak in the Sauerbusch; they are kilometres apart, so it is a ride rather than a stroll. The pin is approximate, and the last dated photographs we know of are from 2017 and 2018. If you go, tell us how it is doing.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its broad crown, part of it broken out by rot and lightning, beside the Brauteich pond. It stands on open land west of Langebrück, north of the railway line.

story:
This oak was planted in 1681 as a timber investment, and nobody ever collected. The parish of Pesterwitz put it in together with several other trees, meaning to sell the wood one day. The others are gone. This one still stands on the bend at the entrance to the village, on the road called An der Winzerei near the church of St. Jakobus.

Its name comes from the calendar rather than from any record of why it went in: 1680 and 1681 were plague years, and the tree became the Pesteiche, the plague oak.

It has come close to the axe since. In the Second World War it was marked to be felled for a tank barrier, and it survived that too. Today it is over 20 metres tall, the regional tourism office says almost 22, with a trunk more than five metres round. The crown needs help to hold together: it is secured with ropes, and another brace went in with the pruning of 2023.

The custom of naming a tree for an epidemic did not end with it. In 2021 a young oak was planted near the old Winzerei and called the Corona oak.

Pesterwitz belongs to the town of Freital, just west of Dresden, which protects the oak as one of its natural monuments. It stands right on the road with no verge or bench, so this is a tree to look up at from the roadside rather than to sit under.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the ropes and brace holding its crown together and the protection sign in front of it. It stands right on the road An der Winzerei, on the bend at the entrance to the village.

story:
The sources disagree about when this oak was planted by two full centuries: somewhere between 1570 and 1770. What they agree on is where. It stands in the Grünes Tälchen, the little green valley of the Hammerbach, on the old boundary between Pesterwitz and Potschappel, and it may have been planted to mark that line. That is how it got its name, the Grenzeiche, the boundary oak.

Whatever its age, it has the build of an old tree. When it was measured in February 2022 its trunk was 6.20 metres round, it stood about 29 metres tall and its crown spread more than 22 metres. The trunk is hollow. Somebody once tried to set fire to it, and it survived; on that same 2022 visit it was recorded as vital, with no fungi.

So the age here is a band rather than a number, roughly 250 to 450 years depending on which local history you follow, and one tree register settles on the low end. If a dated document for the planting exists, we would like to see it.

The oak is one of the natural monuments of the town of Freital, just west of Dresden, and the Plague Oak of Pesterwitz, planted in 1681, stands about a kilometre away. Here the setting is quieter: the bank of a stream, where the public path from Kohlsdorfer Strasse to Kohlsdorf crosses the water.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the hollow trunk, 6.20 metres round. It stands alone on the bank of the Hammerbach, where the path from Kohlsdorfer Strasse to Kohlsdorf crosses the stream.

story:
This pine has watched the forest around it be felled and grown back twice. Foresters count in rotations, the 80 to 140 years between planting a stand and cutting it, and this tree, which the city's documentation estimates at about 250 years old, has outlasted two of them. It was left standing each time, and now rises to about 25 metres over the open high forest of the Dresdner Heide.

It is not a giant. Its trunk is 2.75 metres round and its crown about 12 metres across. What makes it rare is age in a working forest, where pines are grown to be harvested; the estimate puts its start somewhere in the middle or later part of the 18th century.

In the 1970s volunteer naturalists proposed naming it the Karl-Jahn-Kiefer, after the forester who ran the Dresdner Heide forestry office from 1958 to 1975 and pushed for the landscape protection area of 1969. The name never caught on, though a sign bearing it has been photographed on the tree. Dresden made it a natural monument in January 1985, and its protection zone covers the whole crown and at least 18 metres around the trunk.

It stands about 60 metres east of the Weissiger Weg, between the Ochsensteig and the Bischofsweg, with a plaque on its trunk. The most recent dated photographs we know of are from June 2017. If you walk out to it, tell us it is still there.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the natural monument plaque on its trunk and by how it towers over the open forest around it. It stands about 60 metres east of the Weissiger Weg, between the Ochsensteig and the Bischofsweg.
